docs.title: Envizi Integration Hub - Prepare Configuration file
docs.text: This document explains about how to prepare Configuration file to use in Envizi Integration Hub.

docs.title: 1. Download the Config file
docs.text:
1. Download the envizi-integration-hub/api/config/envizi-sample-config.json
  2. Rename it to envizi-config.json

docs.title: 2. Update Envizi s3 bucket details
docs.text:
Update the below envizi s3 bucket details from the data we noted while creating Data service in envizi.

  "envizi": {
    "access": {
      "bucket_name": "envizi-client-dataservice-us-prod",
      "folder_name": "client_9608cd600af647",
      "access_key": "xxxx",
      "secret_key": "xxxxx"
    },
  }

"envizi": { "access": { "bucket_name": "envizi-client-dataservice-us-prod", "folder_name": "client_dedd4566f2f247", "access_key": "xxxx", "secret_key": "xxxx" }, "parameters": { "org_name": "IBM APAC", "org_link": 17000104, "prefix": "G5" } },

docs.title: 3. Update Envizi OrgName
docs.text:
Update org_name in envizi section.

The Org Name is your organization name in the org hierarchy.

  "envizi": {
    "parameters": {
      "org_name": "IBM APAC",
      "org_link": 17000104,
    }
  },

docs.title: 4. Update Envizi Prefix (Optional)
docs.text:
Update prefix in envizi section.

This helps to create all the groups, locations and accounts created by this integration hub prefixed to avoid duplicates if any.

  "envizi": {
    "parameters": {
      "prefix": "G5"
    }
  },

docs.title: 5. Update Turbonomic access
docs.text:
Update the below Turbonomic access details.

The user should have Observer role.

  "turbo": {
    "access": {
      "url": "https://xxxxx.turbonomic.com",
      "user": "",
      "password": ""
    },
  }

docs.title: 6. Update Turbonomic parameters (Optional)
docs.text:
Here are the Turbonomic parameters. You may need to modify account_style_xxxxx properties as per your environment. Otherwise no updates are required in the parameters. You can see the below explanations about the parameters.

  "turbo": {
    "parameters": {
      "group": "Sustainable-IT",
      "sub_group": "Turbonomic",
      "start_date": "2023-10-30",
      "end_date": "2023-11-04"
    },
    }
  1. The group and sub_group are created as Groups in Organization Hierarchy.
  2. Each datacenter from Turbonomic is created as a Location under the sub_group.

docs.title: 7. Update Turbonomic Account Styles (Optional)
docs.text:
You may need to modify account_style_xxxxx properties as per your environment. Otherwise no updates are required in the parameters. You can see the below explanations about the parameters.

  "turbo": {
    "account_styles" : [
      {
        "name": "energy_consumption",
        "link": 14445,
        "account_name": "Energy Consumption", 
        "caption": "S2 - Electricity - kWh", 
        "columns" : ["Total Electricity (kWh)", "Green Power (kWh)", "Total Cost"],
        "file_prefix" : "Account_Setup_and_Data_Load_engery_"
      },
      {
        "name": "active_hosts",
        "link": 17000021,
        ....
        ....
        ....
      }
    ]
    }

Similar to the below Accounts and Account Styles to be created for each Datacenter from Turbonomic. Account Account Style ----------------------- ------------------------ Energy Consumption --- Energy Consumption - kWh Active Hosts --- Active Hosts [Number] Active VMs --- Active Virtual Machines [Number] Energy Host Intensity --- Energy Host Intensity - kWh/host VM Host Density --- Virtual Machine to Host Density - VM/Host

If you have these Account Styles in your environment you can update the account_style_xxxxx properties with the your values.

docs.title: Envizi Integration Hub - Starting the App using Source code
docs.text:
This document explains about how to start Envizi Integration Hub using Source code.

You need to start 2 apps (API app and UI app).

docs.title: 1. Start the Python API App
docs.text:
1. Download this repo.

  2. Prepare Configuration file by using the link 02-prepare-configuration-filed

  3. Keep the property file envizi-config.json in some folder. Lets us assume the file is located in /Users/xyz/envizi-integration-hub-app/api/config/envizi-config.json

  4. Run the below command to create virutal environment (first time only).

python -m venv myvenv
source myvenv/bin/activate

python -m pip install -r requirements.txt

  1. Replace /Users/xyz/envizi-integration-hub-app with your folder structure in the below commands.

  2. Run the below command to start the app.

export WRITE_INTERIM_FILES=FALSE
export LOGLEVEL=INFO
export ENVIZI_CONFIG_FILE="/Users/xyz/envizi-integration-hub-app/api/config/envizi-config.json"
export DATA_FOLDER="/Users/xyz/envizi-integration-hub-app/api/data"
export DATA_STORE_FOLDER="/Users/xyz/envizi-integration-hub-app/api/data-store"

export OUTPUT_FOLDER="/Users/xyz/envizi-integration-hub-app/output"

cd /Users/xyz/envizi-integration-hub-app/api

python src/main.py
  1. Open the url in your browser http://localhost:3001/hello to check if it is working.

Note: If you are running this in VM, then instead of localhost you need to give the IP-Address of your vm.

docs.title: 2. Start the Web App (Reactjs)
docs.text:
We need to pass the URL of the Python API App to the Web App.

  1. Create .env file with the below content under the web folder.
NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL=http://localhost:3001

Note: If you are running this in VM, then instead of localhost you need to give the IP-Address of your vm.

  1. Run the below command build (first time only).
 yarn build
  1. Run the below command to start the app.
yarn run dev
  1. Open the url in your browser http://localhost:3000/

Note: If you are running this in VM, then instead of localhost you need to give the IP-Address of your vm.

docs.title: Starting the App using Docker / Podman
docs.text:
This document explains about how to start Envizi Integration Hub in Docker / Podman.

You need to run the 2 docker images (API app and UI app).

docs.title: 1. Start the API App
docs.text:
Lets start the API App in Linux VM.

  1. Keep the configuration file envizi-config.json in some folder. Lets us assume the file is located in /tmp/envizi-config.json

  2. Run the below command to start the app.

The abolve file name is mentioned in the -v parameter here and suffixed with :/app/envizi-config.json

docker run -d -p 3001:3001 --name my-e-int2-hub \
    --env LOGLEVEL=DEBUG \
    --env DATA_FOLDER="/app/data" \
    --env DATA_STORE_FOLDER="/app/data" \
    --env OUTPUT_FOLDER="/app/output" \
    -v "/tmp/envizi-config.json:/app/envizi-config.json" \
    gandigit/e-int-hub2-linux:latest

docs.title: Note
docs.text:
• To run the same in Mac, you need to change the image e-int-hub2-linux into e-int-hub2-mac in the above command.

  • To run the same using Podman instead of Docker, you need to change the docker into podman in the above command.

  • Open the url http://##IP_ADDRESS_OF_VM##:3001/hello in the browser to see if it is working.

docs.title: 2. Start the UI App
docs.text:
Lets start the UI App in Linux VM.

  1. Replace the ##IP_ADDRESS_OF_VM## with the actual IP address of the VM where API App is running.
podman run -d -p 3000:3000 --name my-e-int-hub2-ui --env NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL="http://##IP_ADDRESS_OF_VM##:3001"  gandigit/e-int-hub2-ui-linux:latest
  1. Run the above command to start the UI app.

docs.title: Note
docs.text:
• To run the same in Mac, you need to change the image e-int-hub2-ui-linux into e-int-hub2-ui-mac in the above command.

  • To run the same using Podman instead of Docker, you need to change the docker into podman in the above command.

  • Open the url http://##IP_ADDRESS_OF_VM##:3000/hello in the browser to see if it is working.

  • The below home page should have been displayed.

docs.title: 3. Stop the App (for info only)
docs.text:
Run the below commands one by one to stop the apps.

docker stop my-e-int2-hub
docker rm my-e-int2-hub

docker stop my-e-int2-hub-ui
docker rm my-e-int2-hub-ui

docs.title: 4. View App logs (for info only)
docs.text:
Run the below commmand to view the logs of the apps.

docker logs my-e-int2-hub

docker logs my-e-int2-hub-ui

docs.title: Frequently Asked Questions
docs.text: Frequently Asked Questions about the Integration Hub.

docs.title: 1. Is this an add-on product/module from Envizi?
docs.text: It is a solution accelerator to integrate ESG data into Envizi. And it is not part of Envizi. From a data flow automation perspective, this is a sample implementation of the Self-Service Pathway.

docs.title: 2. Will this application incur costs for the partners or customers?
docs.text: It is an Open-source application based on APACHE License. There is no cost involved here.

docs.title: 3. How do we install this app?
docs.text:
Partners and Clients can install this accelerator on their environment and kick start the data integrations into Envizi. You can either download and run the source code or use a Docker image to set it up.

https://github.com/ibm-ecosystem-engineering/envizi-integration-hub-app/tree/main/docs/50-developer/03-start-app-in-local

https://github.com/ibm-ecosystem-engineering/envizi-integration-hub-app/tree/main/docs/50-developer/05-run-in-docker

docs.title: 4. Is it allowed to modify or extend the app to implement additional functionality?
docs.text: Being it is an Open-source application this can be extended and used by the Partners and Clients.

docs.title: 5. What are the Technologies used in this app?
docs.text: Python, ReactJS, Carbon theme and Watson Discovery (Optional)

docs.title: 6. What is the System Configuration need to run this app?
docs.text: Windows, Linux or MAC system with 16 GB Ram would be sufficient to run this application

docs.title: 7. Is this app being used by other Partners and Clients?
docs.text: Yes, few partners already started using this app for the ESG data integrations with Envizi.

docs.title: 8. Who developed this app and what is the support available?
docs.text: This was developed by the IBM Ecosystem Engineering SI Lab team. Officially, no support is guaranteed as it is open-source and easily extendable. However, based on resource availability, needs, and feedback, some enhancements and fixes may be considered.

docs.title: 9. What are the integrations available in the app as of now?
docs.text: Given below the list of integrations available. - Excel Integrations - Webhook Integrations (e.g., SAP, ERP Systems) - Invoice Processing - Utility Bill Processing - Turbonomic Integration

docs.title: 10. A partner is supporting more than one client or customer. How many instances of this app to be installed?
docs.text: The configuration section of the app contains the connected Envizi Instance info. So, for each client/customer, the partner needs to have the separate instance of this app.

docs.title: 11. Is there a commercial model planned?
docs.text: This accelerator was built to assist the partners and IBMers to assist them in their presales to demonstrate the integration flows with Envizi from various data sources, however users can extend and can scale based on their needs.

docs.title: 12. Can this application be setup both on Windows and Linux ?
docs.text: Yes, you can set up on Windows, Linux or MAC systems.

docs.title: 13. Would this capability be integration with Envizi?
docs.text: No, this is built as a solution accelerator to compliment the Envizi’s data flow automation framework.

docs.title: 90-blog/readme-developer.md
docs.text:
Integration Hub is a solution accelerator to facilitate the integration of ESG data from various sources into the IBM Envizi ESG Suite. The Hub provides configurable hooks to Integrate with any ESG data source, helps transform and integrate.

[Watch the quick overview video about the Integration Hub.]

It leverage Envizi’s data flow automation capability and align with data templates. There are two pathways ingesting data into Envizi. - On the top it shows ENVIZI SERVICES PATHWAY via Expert Labs which is a paid services. - On the bottom is the SELF SERVICES PATHWAY for clients or partners to take complete ownership DataTransformation and Integration.

Integration Hub is a one of the solution for the SELF SERVICES PATHWAY. As part of this we provide you the Development toolkit to enable the Integration Specialists, Practioners, developers or managed services team to quickly build integration showcases.

The following integrations are available in Integration Hub as of now.

  1. Excel Integrations
  2. WebHook Integrations (SAP, ERP Systems)
  3. Invoice Processing
  4. Utility Bill Processing
  5. Turbonomic Integration

This Integration Hub can be extended to include integration with numerous other external systems that need to interface with the IBM Envizi ESG Suite. It connects to external systems, such as Turbonomic, Webhook API, Watson Discovery and etc, retrieves emissions data, converts this data into the Universal Account Setup and Data Loading format (UDC), and then dispatches it to an S3 bucket configured within the IBM Envizi ESG Suite.

The entire source code and detailed documentation of this application is available here.

You can find more detailed information in section below on each of the integrations, how to deploy, run and extend the application further based on your need.

docs.title: Integration Hub
docs.text:
(Solution Accelerator for IBM Envizi)

Integration Hub is a solution accelerator to facilitates the integration of ESG data from various sources into the IBM Envizi ESG Suite.

The Hub provides configurable hooks to Integrate with any ESG data source, helps transform and integrate.

It leverage Envizi’s data flow automation capability and align with data templates.

There are two pathways ingesting data into Envizi. - On the top it shows ENVIZI SERVICES PATHWAY via Expert Labs which is a paid services. - On the bottom is the SELF SERVICES PATHWAY for clients or partners to take complete ownership DataTransformation and Integration.

Integration Hub is a one of the solution for the SELF SERVICES PATHWAY.

The following integrations are available in Integration Hub as of now.

  1. Excel Integrations
  2. WebHook Integrations (SAP, ERP Systems)
  3. Invoice Processing
  4. Utility Bill Processing
  5. Turbonomic Integration

This Integration Hub can be extended to include integration with numerous other external systems that need to interface with the IBM Envizi ESG Suite.

It connects to external systems, such as Turbonomic, Webhook API, Watson Discovery and etc, retrieves emissions data, converts this data into the Universal Account Setup and Data Loading format (UDC), and then dispatches it to an S3 bucket configured within the IBM Envizi ESG Suite.

The entire source code and detailed documentation of this application is available in https://github.com/ibm-ecosystem-engineering/envizi-integration-hub-app/tree/main.

We have highlighted few key information in this article.

docs.title: 1. Is this an add-on product/module from Envizi?
docs.text: It is a solution accelerator to integrate ESG data into Envizi. And it is not part of Envizi. From a data flow automation perspective, this is a sample implementation of the Self-Service Pathway.

docs.title: 2. Will this application incur costs for the partners or customers?
docs.text: It is an Open-source application based on APACHE License. There is no cost involved here.

docs.title: 3. How do we install this app?
docs.text:
Partners and Clients can install this accelerator on their environment and kick start the data integrations into Envizi. You can either download and run the source code or use a Docker image to set it up.

https://github.com/ibm-ecosystem-engineering/envizi-integration-hub-app/tree/main/docs/50-developer/03-start-app-in-local

docs.title: 4. Is it allowed to modify or extend the app to implement additional functionality?
docs.text: Being it is an Open-source application this can be extended and used by the Partners and Clients.

docs.title: 5. What are the Technologies used in this app?
docs.text: Python, ReactJS, Carbon theme and Watson Discovery (Optional)

docs.title: 6. What is the System Configuration need to run this app?
docs.text: Windows, Linux or MAC system with 16 GB Ram would be sufficient to run this application

docs.title: 7. Is this app being used by other Partners and Clients?
docs.text: Yes, few partners already started using this app for the ESG data integrations with Envizi.

docs.title: 8. Who developed this app and what is the support available?
docs.text: This was developed by the IBM Ecosystem Engineering SI Lab team. Officially, no support is guaranteed as it is open-source and easily extendable. However, based on resource availability, needs, and feedback, some enhancements and fixes may be considered.

docs.title: 9. What are the integrations available in the app as of now?
docs.text: Given below the list of integrations available. - Excel Integrations - Webhook Integrations (e.g., SAP, ERP Systems) - Invoice Processing - Utility Bill Processing - Turbonomic Integration

docs.title: 10. A partner is supporting more than one client or customer. How many instances of this app to be installed?
docs.text: The configuration section of the app contains the connected Envizi Instance info. So, for each client/customer, the partner needs to have the separate instance of this app.

docs.title: 11. Is there a commercial model planned?
docs.text: This accelerator was built to assist the partners and IBMers to assist them in their presales to demonstrate the integration flows with Envizi from various data sources, however users can extend and can scale based on their needs.

docs.title: 12. Can this application be setup both on Windows and Linux ?
docs.text: Yes, you can set up on Windows, Linux or MAC systems.

docs.title: 13. Would this capability be integration with Envizi?
docs.text: No, this is built as a solution accelerator to compliment the Envizi’s data flow automation framework.

Integration Hub is a solution accelerator to facilitate the integration of ESG data from various sources into the IBM Envizi ESG Suite. The Hub provides configurable hooks to Integrate with any ESG data source, helps transform and integrate.

[Watch the quick overview video about the Integration Hub.]

It leverage Envizi’s data flow automation capability and align with data templates. There are two pathways ingesting data into Envizi. - On the top it shows ENVIZI SERVICES PATHWAY via Expert Labs which is a paid services. - On the bottom is the SELF SERVICES PATHWAY for clients or partners to take complete ownership DataTransformation and Integration.

Integration Hub is a one of the solution for the SELF SERVICES PATHWAY. As part of this we provide you the Development toolkit to enable the Integration Specialists, Practioners, developers or managed services team to quickly build integration showcases.

The following integrations are available in Integration Hub as of now.

  1. Excel Integrations
  2. WebHook Integrations (SAP, ERP Systems)
  3. Invoice Processing
  4. Utility Bill Processing
  5. Turbonomic Integration

This Integration Hub can be extended to include integration with numerous other external systems that need to interface with the IBM Envizi ESG Suite. It connects to external systems, such as Turbonomic, Webhook API, Watson Discovery and etc, retrieves emissions data, converts this data into the Universal Account Setup and Data Loading format (UDC), and then dispatches it to an S3 bucket configured within the IBM Envizi ESG Suite.

The entire source code and detailed documentation of this application is available here.

You can find more detailed information in section below on each of the integrations, how to deploy, run and extend the application further based on your need.

docs.title: Integration Hub
docs.text:
(Solution Accelerator for IBM Envizi)

Integration Hub is a solution accelerator to facilitates the integration of ESG data from various sources into the IBM Envizi ESG Suite.

The Hub provides configurable hooks to Integrate with any ESG data source, helps transform and integrate.

It leverage Envizi’s data flow automation capability and align with data templates.

There are two pathways ingesting data into Envizi. - On the top it shows ENVIZI SERVICES PATHWAY via Expert Labs which is a paid services. - On the bottom is the SELF SERVICES PATHWAY for clients or partners to take complete ownership DataTransformation and Integration.

Integration Hub is a one of the solution for the SELF SERVICES PATHWAY.

The following integrations are available in Integration Hub as of now.

  1. Excel Integrations
  2. WebHook Integrations (SAP, ERP Systems)
  3. Invoice Processing
  4. Utility Bill Processing
  5. Turbonomic Integration

This Integration Hub can be extended to include integration with numerous other external systems that need to interface with the IBM Envizi ESG Suite.

It connects to external systems, such as Turbonomic, Webhook API, Watson Discovery and etc, retrieves emissions data, converts this data into the Universal Account Setup and Data Loading format (UDC), and then dispatches it to an S3 bucket configured within the IBM Envizi ESG Suite.

The entire source code and detailed documentation of this application is available in https://github.com/ibm-ecosystem-engineering/envizi-integration-hub-app/tree/main.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: This document outlines the software, credentials, and network requirements needed to deploy the Ollama service on Open Horizon edge nodes.

docs.title: Open Horizon Agent
docs.text:
The Open Horizon agent must be installed and configured on your edge node.

Supported Versions: - Open Horizon Agent 2.30.0 or later

Installation: - Follow the Open Horizon Agent Installation Guide - Verify installation: hzn version

docs.title: Container Runtime
docs.text:
A container runtime is required to run the Ollama service container.

Supported Runtimes: - Docker 20.10 or later - Podman 3.0 or later

Installation: - Docker: Install Docker Engine - Podman: Install Podman

Verify Installation:

docker --version
# or
podman --version

docs.title: System Requirements
docs.text:
Minimum Hardware: - CPU: 2 cores - RAM: 2 GB minimum, 4 GB recommended - Storage: 10 GB minimum, 20 GB recommended for models - Architecture: x86_64 (amd64) or ARM64

Operating System: - Linux (Ubuntu 20.04+, RHEL 8+, Debian 11+) - macOS 11+ (for development/testing)

docs.title: Open Horizon Exchange Credentials
docs.text:
You need valid credentials to access the Open Horizon Exchange.

Required Information: - Organization ID (HZN_ORG_ID) - Exchange URL (HZN_EXCHANGE_URL) - User credentials (HZN_EXCHANGE_USER_AUTH in format user:password or user:api-key)

Obtain Credentials: - Contact your Open Horizon administrator - Or register at your organization's Exchange instance

Set Environment Variables:

export HZN_ORG_ID="your-org-id"
export HZN_EXCHANGE_URL="https://exchange.example.com/v1"
export HZN_EXCHANGE_USER_AUTH="your-user:your-password"

docs.title: Service Signing Keys (Optional)
docs.text:
If you plan to publish services, you need RSA key pairs for signing.

Generate Keys:

hzn key create "your-company" "your-email@example.com"

This creates: - ~/.hzn/keys/service.private.key - ~/.hzn/keys/service.public.pem

docs.title: Outbound Connectivity
docs.text:
The edge node must have outbound network access to:

Open Horizon Services: - Exchange API (typically port 443/HTTPS) - Agbot API (typically port 443/HTTPS) - CSS (Cloud Sync Service) if used (typically port 443/HTTPS)

Container Registry: - Docker Hub (docker.io) for pulling Ollama images - Port 443/HTTPS

Bandwidth Considerations: - Initial Ollama container image: ~1-2 GB - Model downloads: varies by model (500 MB to 10+ GB) - Recommend stable connection with at least 10 Mbps for initial setup

docs.title: Inbound Connectivity (Optional)
docs.text:
If you want to access the Ollama API from external clients: - Port 11434/TCP (Ollama API default port)

Firewall Configuration:

# Example for UFW (Ubuntu)
sudo ufw allow 11434/tcp

# Example for firewalld (RHEL/CentOS)
sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-port=11434/tcp
sudo firewall-cmd --reload

docs.title: Persistent Storage for Models
docs.text:
Ollama stores models in /root/.ollama by default. For production deployments, configure persistent storage.

Recommended Approach: - Create a dedicated volume or directory - Mount it to the container at /root/.ollama

Example Setup:

# Create directory for model storage
sudo mkdir -p /var/ollama
sudo chmod 755 /var/ollama

# Or create a Docker volume
docker volume create ollama-storage

The service definition includes this configuration by default.

docs.title: Verification Checklist
docs.text:
Before proceeding with deployment, verify:

  • [ ] Open Horizon agent installed and running (hzn version)
  • [ ] Container runtime installed (docker --version or podman --version)
  • [ ] System meets minimum hardware requirements
  • [ ] Exchange credentials configured and tested (hzn exchange status)
  • [ ] Network connectivity to Exchange and Docker Hub
  • [ ] Persistent storage configured (if required)
  • [ ] Firewall rules configured (if external access needed)

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text: Once all prerequisites are met, proceed to the Quick Start Guide for deployment instructions.

docs.title: Agent Not Connecting to Exchange
docs.text:
Symptom: hzn exchange status fails or times out

Solutions: 1. Verify Exchange URL is correct 2. Check network connectivity: curl -sS $HZN_EXCHANGE_URL/status 3. Verify credentials are correct 4. Check firewall rules allow outbound HTTPS

docs.title: Container Runtime Issues
docs.text:
Symptom: Docker/Podman commands fail

Solutions: 1. Verify service is running: sudo systemctl status docker 2. Check user permissions: Add user to docker group 3. Restart service: sudo systemctl restart docker

docs.title: Insufficient Storage
docs.text:
Symptom: Container fails to start or model downloads fail

Solutions: 1. Check available space: df -h 2. Clean up unused containers: docker system prune 3. Move model storage to larger volume

docs.title: Quick Start Guide
docs.text: This guide provides step-by-step instructions for deploying the Ollama service on Open Horizon edge nodes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Before starting, ensure you have completed all items in the Prerequisites document.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The deployment process consists of: 1. Publishing the service to the Exchange 2. Publishing service and deployment policies 3. Registering your edge node 4. Verifying the deployment

docs.title: Step 1: Configure Environment
docs.text:
Set required environment variables for your deployment:

# Your Open Horizon organization ID
export HZN_ORG_ID="your-org-id"

# Exchange API endpoint
export HZN_EXCHANGE_URL="https://exchange.example.com/v1"

# Your Exchange credentials (user:password or user:api-key)
export HZN_EXCHANGE_USER_AUTH="your-user:your-password"

# Target architecture (amd64 or arm64)
export ARCH="amd64"

# Service version
export SERVICE_VERSION="0.1.0"

Verify Configuration:

hzn exchange status

Expected Output:

Exchange URL: https://exchange.example.com/v1
Exchange version: 2.87.0
Exchange root user: root/root
Your user: your-org-id/your-user

docs.title: Step 2: Validate Service Definition
docs.text:
Before publishing, validate the service definition files:

cd /path/to/service-ollama
make validate-service

Expected Output:

=======================
VALIDATING SERVICE
=======================
Service definition validated successfully

If Validation Fails: - Check JSON syntax in horizon/service.definition.json - Verify all required fields are present - Ensure environment variables are set correctly

docs.title: Step 3: Publish Service to Exchange
docs.text:
Publish the Ollama service definition to the Open Horizon Exchange:

make publish-service

Expected Output:

==================
PUBLISHING SERVICE
==================
Publishing service definition...
Service published: your-org-id/service-ollama_0.1.0_amd64

Verify Publication:

make list-services

You should see your service listed in the output.

docs.title: Step 4: Publish Service Policy
docs.text:
Publish the service policy that defines service-side constraints:

make publish-service-policy

Expected Output:

=========================
PUBLISHING SERVICE POLICY
=========================
Service policy published for: your-org-id/service-ollama_0.1.0_amd64

docs.title: Step 5: Publish Deployment Policy
docs.text:
Publish the deployment policy that defines where and how the service should be deployed:

make publish-deployment-policy

Expected Output:

============================
PUBLISHING DEPLOYMENT POLICY
============================
Deployment policy published: your-org-id/policy-service-ollama_0.1.0

docs.title: Step 6: Configure Node Policy
docs.text:
Before registering your node, review and customize the node policy if needed:

cat horizon/node.policy.json

Key Configuration Items: - openhorizon.memory: Available memory in MB (default: 4096) - openhorizon.storage: Available storage in MB (default: 20480) - openhorizon.arch: Node architecture (amd64 or arm64)

Edit if Necessary:

# Update memory value
sed -i 's/"value": 4096/"value": 8192/' horizon/node.policy.json

# Update architecture for ARM64 nodes
sed -i 's/"value": "amd64"/"value": "arm64"/' horizon/node.policy.json

docs.title: Step 7: Register Edge Node

Register your edge node with the node policy:

make agent-run

What Happens: 1. Node registers with the Exchange 2. Node policy is applied 3. Agreement negotiation begins 4. Service container is deployed

Expected Output:

================
REGISTERING NODE
================

Node registered successfully
Waiting for agreement...

The command will watch for agreement formation. Press Ctrl+C when you see an agreement listed.

docs.title: Service Not Starting
docs.text:
Symptom: No container running after registration

Check:

hzn eventlog list

Common Causes: - Insufficient resources (memory/storage) - Network connectivity issues - Policy mismatch between node and deployment

Solution: 1. Verify node meets resource requirements 2. Check node policy matches deployment policy constraints 3. Review event log for specific errors

docs.title: Agreement Not Forming
docs.text:
Symptom: hzn agreement list shows no agreements

Check:

hzn deploycheck all -t device -B horizon/deployment.policy.json \
  --service=horizon/service.definition.json \
  --service-pol=horizon/service.policy.json \
  --node-pol=horizon/node.policy.json

Common Causes: - Policy constraints don't match - Service not published correctly - Node properties don't satisfy deployment policy

Solution: 1. Run deploycheck to identify mismatches 2. Adjust node policy or deployment policy as needed 3. Re-register node if policy changes

docs.title: Container Fails to Pull
docs.text:
Symptom: Agreement formed but container not running

Check:

docker pull ollama/ollama:latest

Common Causes: - No internet connectivity - Docker Hub rate limiting - Insufficient disk space

Solution: 1. Verify network connectivity to Docker Hub 2. Check available disk space: df -h 3. Wait and retry if rate limited

docs.title: API Access and Integration
docs.text: This guide covers procedures for accessing the Ollama API from edge applications and verifying API functionality.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The Ollama service exposes a REST API on port 11434 for model inference and management. This guide covers API connectivity, authentication, and common integration patterns.

docs.title: API Endpoint
docs.text:
Default Endpoint: http://localhost:11434

Available from: - Same host as container - Other containers on same network - External clients (if firewall configured)

docs.title: Basic Connectivity Test

}

If Connection Fails:

docs.title: Current Status
docs.text: Ollama does not currently support built-in authentication. The API is open to anyone who can reach the endpoint.

docs.title: Option 1: Network-Level Security
docs.text:
# Restrict access to specific IPs
sudo iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 11434 -s 192.168.1.0/24 -j ACCEPT
sudo iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 11434 -j DROP

# Or with UFW
sudo ufw allow from 192.168.1.0/24 to any port 11434
sudo ufw deny 11434

docs.title: Option 2: Reverse Proxy with Authentication
docs.text:
Using Nginx:

# /etc/nginx/sites-available/ollama
server {
    listen 8080;

    location / {
        auth_basic "Ollama API";
        auth_basic_user_file /etc/nginx/.htpasswd;

        proxy_pass http://localhost:11434;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
    }
}

Create password file:

sudo apt-get install apache2-utils
sudo htpasswd -c /etc/nginx/.htpasswd admin
sudo systemctl restart nginx

Access with authentication:

curl -u admin:password http://localhost:8080/api/version

docs.title: Python Integration
docs.text:
import requests
import json

class OllamaClient:
    def __init__(self, base_url="http://localhost:11434"):
        self.base_url = base_url

    def generate(self, model, prompt, stream=False):
        """Generate text from prompt"""
        url = f"{self.base_url}/api/generate"
        data = {
            "model": model,
            "prompt": prompt,
            "stream": stream
        }

        response = requests.post(url, json=data)

        if stream:
            for line in response.iter_lines():
                if line:
                    yield json.loads(line)
        else:
            return response.json()

    def chat(self, model, messages, stream=False):
        """Chat with context"""
        url = f"{self.base_url}/api/chat"
        data = {
            "model": model,
            "messages": messages,
            "stream": stream
        }

        response = requests.post(url, json=data)
        return response.json()

    def list_models(self):
        """List available models"""
        url = f"{self.base_url}/api/tags"
        response = requests.get(url)
        return response.json()

# Usage
client = OllamaClient()

# Generate text
result = client.generate("llama2", "Why is the sky blue?")
print(result["response"])

# Chat
messages = [
    {"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}
]
response = client.chat("llama2", messages)
print(response["message"]["content"])

# List models
models = client.list_models()
for model in models["models"]:
    print(f"{model['name']}: {model['size']} bytes")

import time
import requests

def generate_with_retry(model, prompt, max_retries=3):
    for attempt in range(max_retries):
        try:
            response = requests.post(
                'http://localhost:11434/api/generate',
                json={'model': model, 'prompt': prompt, 'stream': False},
                timeout=30
            )
            response.raise_for_status()
            return response.json()
        except requests.exceptions.RequestException as e:
            if attempt == max_retries - 1:
                raise
            time.sleep(2 ** attempt)  # Exponential backoff

docs.text: This guide covers Day 2 operations for managing Ollama models on deployed edge nodes.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Ollama models are managed independently from the service container. This allows you to add, remove, and update models without redeploying the service.

docs.title: Updating Existing Models
docs.text:
Models are updated by pulling the latest version:

# Access the container
docker exec -it $(docker ps -qf "ancestor=ollama/ollama:latest") /bin/bash

# Pull the latest version (will update if newer available)
ollama pull llama2:latest

Update Process: 1. Ollama checks for newer version 2. Downloads only changed layers (efficient) 3. Replaces old version with new version 4. Old version is automatically removed

Example Output:

pulling 8c17c2ebb0ea... 100% ▕████████████████▏ 7.1 KB (updated)

success

# List all models
ollama list | tail -n +2 | awk '{print $1}' > models.txt

# Update each model
while read model; do
  echo "Updating $model..."
  ollama pull "$model"
done < models.txt

docs.text:
1. Plan Storage Capacity:
  2. Small models: 1-3 GB each
  3. Medium models: 4-8 GB each
  4. Large models: 10-40 GB each

  5. Reserve 20% extra for temporary files

  6. Regular Cleanup: bash # Remove unused models monthly ollama list ollama rm <unused-model>

  7. Monitor Storage: bash # Set up monitoring alert THRESHOLD=80 USAGE=$(df -h /var/ollama | tail -1 | awk '{print $5}' | sed 's/%//') if [ $USAGE -gt $THRESHOLD ]; then echo "Warning: Storage usage at ${USAGE}%" fi

docs.title: Example 3: Batch Model Update Script
docs.text:
#!/bin/bash
# update-models.sh

MODELS=(
  "llama2:latest"
  "mistral:latest"
  "codellama:7b"
)

for model in "${MODELS[@]}"; do
  echo "Updating $model..."
  docker exec $(docker ps -qf "ancestor=ollama/ollama:latest") \
    ollama pull "$model"

  if [ $? -eq 0 ]; then
    echo "✓ $model updated successfully"
  else
    echo "✗ Failed to update $model"
  fi
done

echo "Update complete"

#!/bin/bash
# alert.sh

# Thresholds
CPU_THRESHOLD=80
MEM_THRESHOLD=80
DISK_THRESHOLD=85

# Check CPU
CPU_USAGE=$(docker stats --no-stream $(docker ps -qf "ancestor=ollama/ollama:latest") --format "{{.CPUPerc}}" | sed 's/%//')
if (( $(echo "$CPU_USAGE > $CPU_THRESHOLD" | bc -l) )); then
  echo "ALERT: High CPU usage: ${CPU_USAGE}%"
fi

# Check Memory
MEM_USAGE=$(docker stats --no-stream $(docker ps -qf "ancestor=ollama/ollama:latest") --format "{{.MemPerc}}" | sed 's/%//')
if (( $(echo "$MEM_USAGE > $MEM_THRESHOLD" | bc -l) )); then
  echo "ALERT: High memory usage: ${MEM_USAGE}%"
fi

# Check Disk
DISK_USAGE=$(df -h /var/ollama | tail -1 | awk '{print $5}' | sed 's/%//')
if [ "$DISK_USAGE" -gt "$DISK_THRESHOLD" ]; then
  echo "ALERT: High disk usage: ${DISK_USAGE}%"
fi

# Check API
if ! curl -sf http://localhost:11434/api/version > /dev/null; then
  echo "ALERT: API not responding"
fi

docs.title: Storage Management
docs.text: This guide covers procedures for managing persistent model storage across service updates and node restarts.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Ollama stores models in persistent storage to ensure they remain available across container restarts and service updates. Proper storage management is critical for reliable operation.

docs.title: Default Storage Configuration
docs.text:
The Ollama service uses the following storage configuration:

Host Path: /var/ollama Container Path: /root/.ollama Mount Type: Bind mount (read-write)

Service Definition:

{
  "deployment": {
    "services": {
      "ollama": {
        "binds": [
          "/var/ollama:/root/.ollama:rw"
        ]
      }
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Storage Layout
docs.text:
/var/ollama/
├── models/
│   ├── manifests/
│   │   └── registry.ollama.ai/
│   │       └── library/
│   │           ├── llama2/
│   │           ├── mistral/
│   │           └── codellama/
│   └── blobs/
│       ├── sha256-abc123...
│       ├── sha256-def456...
│       └── sha256-ghi789...
└── tmp/

Key Directories: - models/manifests/: Model metadata and version information - models/blobs/: Actual model data (deduplicated) - tmp/: Temporary files during model downloads

#!/bin/bash
# backup-models.sh

BACKUP_DIR="/backup/ollama"
SOURCE_DIR="/var/ollama"
RETENTION_DAYS=30

# Create backup directory
mkdir -p "$BACKUP_DIR"

# Create backup
BACKUP_FILE="$BACKUP_DIR/models-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S).tar.gz"
echo "Creating backup: $BACKUP_FILE"
tar -czf "$BACKUP_FILE" -C "$SOURCE_DIR" models

# Verify backup
if [ $? -eq 0 ]; then
  echo "✓ Backup created successfully"
  ls -lh "$BACKUP_FILE"
else
  echo "✗ Backup failed"
  exit 1
fi

# Remove old backups
echo "Removing backups older than $RETENTION_DAYS days"
find "$BACKUP_DIR" -name "models-*.tar.gz" -mtime +$RETENTION_DAYS -delete

echo "Backup complete"

# Edit crontab
crontab -e

# Add daily backup at 2 AM

#!/bin/bash
# monitor-storage.sh

while true; do
  USAGE=$(df -h /var/ollama | tail -1 | awk '{print $5}' | sed 's/%//')
  USED=$(df -h /var/ollama | tail -1 | awk '{print $3}')
  AVAIL=$(df -h /var/ollama | tail -1 | awk '{print $4}')

  fi

  sleep 3600  # Check every hour
done

Feature Model Context Protocol (MCP) LangChain / LlamaIndex Fundamental Nature An open protocol defining a standard for communication, much like a "USB-C port for AI". A framework or library providing components and structures to build complex AI applications. Purpose Standardize connectivity between AI models and external tools or data sources. Orchestrate complex workflows and manage the internal logic of the AI application. Key Function Provides a standardized interface for accessing tools and data, abstracting away integration details. Offers building blocks for prompt management, chaining, data retrieval (RAG), and agent creation. Best Used For providing standardized, plug-and-play access to a wide range of external tools and data sources. For building complex, stateful applications that require detailed workflow management, advanced reasoning, and memory. Typical Integration Can be used by frameworks like LangChain or LlamaIndex to simplify tool integration. Uses tools (which may be MCP-compliant) as components within its orchestration logic.

docs.title: Supercharging Open Horizon Management with Claude and IBM CodeEngine MCP: A Practical Guide
Introduction
docs.text:
In the rapidly evolving landscape of edge computing, managing distributed devices efficiently has become a critical challenge. Open Horizon, an open-source edge computing platform, provides powerful tools for deploying and managing workloads across edge devices. However, interacting with these tools traditionally requires specialized knowledge and command-line expertise.

Enter the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and large language models like Claude. Together, they transform how we interact with complex systems like Open Horizon, making them accessible through natural language conversations. This blog post explores how to set up and use an Open Horizon MCP server, both locally and in IBM Cloud Code Engine, to enable AI-assisted edge computing management.

By the end of this guide, you'll understand: - What MCP is and why it's valuable for Open Horizon management - How to run the Open Horizon MCP server locally - How to deploy the server to IBM Cloud Code Engine and leverage its serverless capabilities - How to configure Claude Desktop to interact with your MCP server - How to use Claude to manage your Open Horizon environment through natural language

Let's dive in and explore how these technologies can work together to simplify edge computing management.

docs.title: Understanding MCP and Its Value Proposition
What is the Model Context Protocol (MCP)?
docs.text:
The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard that enables AI models to interact with external tools and data sources in a structured way. Think of it as a "USB-C port for AI" - a standardized interface that allows AI assistants like Claude to connect to various systems and perform actions on your behalf.

Unlike traditional APIs that require developers to write code for each integration, MCP provides a consistent way for AI models to: - Discover available tools and capabilities - Execute operations with proper parameters - Receive structured responses - Maintain context across interactions

docs.title: Why MCP Matters for Open Horizon
docs.text:
Open Horizon is a powerful edge computing platform, but its management often requires specialized knowledge and command-line expertise. By exposing Open Horizon's capabilities through an MCP server, we create several key benefits:

  1. Simplified Management: Users can interact with Open Horizon using natural language rather than memorizing complex commands.

  2. Knowledge Democratization: The expertise needed to manage edge devices becomes accessible to team members without specialized training.

  3. Operational Efficiency: Tasks that previously required multiple steps and careful syntax can be accomplished through simple conversational requests.

  4. Reduced Training Requirements: New team members can become productive faster, with the AI guiding them through complex operations.

  5. Better Decision Making: The AI can provide contextual explanations and recommendations based on the current state of your edge environment.

As stated in the Open Horizon MCP Server's value proposition document:

"Exposing Open Horizon's capabilities through an MCP server enables AI agents to autonomously deploy, update, and manage containerized workloads across large numbers of distributed edge devices. Unlike traditional chatbots which rely on static knowledge and require explicit user requests, an MCP-enabled agent can manage and reason across thousands of edge devices simultaneously using real-time data to make dynamic decisions and trigger self-healing actions or re-task devices based on changing needs."

Now that we understand the value, let's see how to set up and use this powerful combination of technologies.

docs.title: Setting Up and Running the Open Horizon MCP Server Locally
docs.text: Running the Open Horizon MCP server locally is a great way to get started with AI-assisted edge computing management. It allows you to test the functionality in a controlled environment before deploying to production. Let's walk through the process step by step.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before we begin, make sure you have the following installed:

  • Node.js (v16 or higher)
  • npm (v7 or higher)
  • Git for cloning the repository
  • Access to an Open Horizon Exchange instance (you'll need the URL and credentials)

docs.title: Step 1: Clone the Repository
docs.text:
First, let's clone the Open Horizon MCP server repository:

git clone https://github.com/your-org/open-horizon-mcp-server.git
cd open-horizon-mcp-server

docs.title: Step 2: Install Dependencies
docs.text:
Next, install the required Node.js dependencies:

npm install

docs.title: Step 3: Configure Environment Variables
docs.text:
The MCP server needs to connect to your Open Horizon Exchange instance. Create a .env file in the root directory with the following variables:

EXCHANGE_URL=<your-exchange-url>
EXCHANGE_ORG=<your-organization>
EXCHANGE_CREDENTIAL=<your-base64-encoded-credentials>
PORT=3000

For example:

EXCHANGE_URL=http://open-horizon.example.com:3091/v1/orgs
EXCHANGE_ORG=myorg
EXCHANGE_CREDENTIAL=bXlvcmcvbXl1c2VyOnBhc3N3b3Jk
PORT=3000

The EXCHANGE_CREDENTIAL should be a Base64-encoded string of your username and password in the format org/user:password. You can generate this using:

echo -n "myorg/myuser:password" | base64

docs.title: Step 4: Build the Project
docs.text:
Compile the TypeScript code:

npm run build

docs.title: Step 5: Start the Server
docs.text:
Now you can start the MCP server:

npm start

You should see output similar to:

Open Horizon MCP Server listening on port: 3000

docs.title: Step 6: Verify the Server is Running
docs.text:
To verify that the server is running correctly, you can check the health endpoint:

curl http://localhost:3000/health

You should receive a response like:

{"status":"healthy"}

docs.title: Understanding the Local Server Architecture
docs.text:
When running locally, the Open Horizon MCP server:

  1. Listens on the configured port (default: 3000) for incoming MCP requests
  2. Maintains stateful sessions for each client connection
  3. Authenticates with the Open Horizon Exchange using the provided credentials
  4. Exposes tools for managing nodes, services, and policies

The server implements the Model Context Protocol, which allows AI assistants like Claude to discover and use the available tools. Each tool is registered with:

  • A unique name (e.g., list-nodes)
  • A description that helps the AI understand when to use it
  • A schema defining the expected parameters
  • A callback function that executes the actual API calls to the Open Horizon Exchange

This architecture makes it easy to extend the server with new capabilities by adding additional tools in the src/tools directory.

Now that we have our server running locally, let's look at how to deploy it to the cloud for production use.

docs.title: Deploying the Open Horizon MCP Server to IBM Cloud Code Engine
docs.text:
While running the MCP server locally is great for development and testing, deploying it to IBM Cloud Code Engine provides significant advantages for production use. Code Engine is a fully managed, serverless platform that's ideal for hosting MCP servers because it offers:

  • Zero infrastructure management - focus on your code, not servers
  • Automatic scaling - from zero to thousands of instances based on demand
  • Cost efficiency - pay only for what you use, with scale-to-zero when idle
  • Built-in security - secure container execution and network isolation
  • Global availability - deploy close to your users for lower latency

docs.title: Prerequisites for Cloud Deployment
docs.text:
Before deploying to IBM Cloud Code Engine, you'll need:

  • IBM Cloud account with Code Engine service enabled
  • IBM Cloud CLI installed and configured
  • Docker installed for building container images
  • Container Registry access (IBM Container Registry or another registry)

docs.title: Step 1: Prepare for Deployment
docs.text:
The Open Horizon MCP server includes a deployment script in the bin/deploy.js file that simplifies the process. Before using it, you'll need to create a configuration file for your environment.

Create a file named .env-local.json in the root directory with your IBM Cloud Code Engine configuration:

{
  "dev": {
    "EXCHANGE_URL": "http://your-exchange-url:3091/v1/orgs",
    "EXCHANGE_ORG": "your-organization",
    "EXCHANGE_CREDENTIAL": "your-base64-encoded-credentials",
    "REGISTRY_ACCESS_SECRET": "your-registry-secret-name"
  },
  "prod": {
    "EXCHANGE_URL": "http://your-production-exchange-url:3091/v1/orgs",
    "EXCHANGE_ORG": "your-organization",
    "EXCHANGE_CREDENTIAL": "your-base64-encoded-credentials",
    "REGISTRY_ACCESS_SECRET": "your-registry-secret-name"
  }
}

docs.title: Step 2: Build and Push the Docker Image
docs.text:
The Open Horizon MCP server uses a multi-stage Dockerfile that creates an optimized container image. The deployment script handles building and pushing the image to your container registry.

To build for AMD64 architecture (most cloud environments):

npm run build:docker:amd64

For ARM64 architecture:

npm run build:docker:arm64

docs.title: Step 3: Deploy to IBM Cloud Code Engine
docs.text:
Once your Docker image is built and pushed to the registry, you can deploy to Code Engine using the provided script:

# Deploy to development environment
npm run deploy:dev

# Or deploy to production environment
npm run deploy:prod

These commands use the bin/deploy.js script, which:

  1. Builds the TypeScript code
  2. Creates a Docker image for the specified platform
  3. Tags the image with your registry information
  4. Pushes the image to the container registry
  5. Creates or updates the Code Engine application with the new image
  6. Sets environment variables from your .env-local.json file

docs.title: Step 4: Verify the Deployment
docs.text:
After deployment, you can verify that your MCP server is running in Code Engine:

# Get the application URL
npm run --appname=open-horizon-mcp-server-dev appUrl

# Check the application status
npm run --appname=open-horizon-mcp-server-dev appInfo

# View application logs
npm run --appname=open-horizon-mcp-server-dev appLogs

The application URL will be something like:

https://open-horizon-mcp-server-dev.abcdefgh.us-south.codeengine.appdomain.cloud

You can verify the server is running by checking the health endpoint:

curl https://open-horizon-mcp-server-dev.abcdefgh.us-south.codeengine.appdomain.cloud/health

docs.title: Benefits of IBM Cloud Code Engine for MCP Servers
docs.text:
Deploying your Open Horizon MCP server to IBM Cloud Code Engine offers several key advantages:

  1. Elastic Scalability: Code Engine automatically scales your MCP server based on incoming requests. During periods of high demand (like when multiple users are interacting with Claude), it scales up to handle the load. When traffic decreases, it scales down to save costs—even to zero when not in use.

  2. Global Availability: Deploy your MCP server in multiple regions to reduce latency for users around the world. This is especially valuable for organizations with globally distributed edge devices and teams.

  3. Simplified Operations: Code Engine eliminates the need to manage servers, containers, or Kubernetes clusters. This reduces operational overhead and lets you focus on enhancing your MCP server's capabilities.

  4. Cost Optimization: With the pay-per-use model, you only pay for the actual compute resources consumed during request processing. For MCP servers that handle intermittent requests, this can result in significant cost savings compared to always-on deployments.

  5. Enterprise-Grade Security: Code Engine provides built-in security features like private networking, secrets management, and integration with IBM Cloud IAM for access control.

docs.title: Leveraging Code Engine Fleet (Coming Soon)
docs.text:
IBM Cloud Code Engine is introducing a new feature called "Fleet" that will be particularly valuable for MCP server deployments:

  1. Multi-Region Deployment: Fleet will allow you to deploy your MCP server across multiple regions with a single command, ensuring high availability and disaster recovery.

  2. Intelligent Traffic Routing: Requests will be automatically routed to the nearest healthy instance, reducing latency for users regardless of their location.

  3. Consistent Configuration: Fleet will maintain consistent configuration across all regions, simplifying management of your global MCP server deployment.

  4. Centralized Monitoring: Get a unified view of your MCP server's performance and usage across all regions, making it easier to identify and resolve issues.

When Code Engine Fleet becomes available, you'll be able to enhance your MCP server deployment with these capabilities, making it even more resilient and responsive for users around the world.

docs.title: Understanding the Cloud Deployment Architecture
docs.text:
When deployed to IBM Cloud Code Engine, the Open Horizon MCP server:

  1. Runs as a containerized application using the Docker image we built
  2. Scales automatically based on incoming traffic (even to zero when not in use)
  3. Maintains high availability through Code Engine's infrastructure
  4. Securely stores credentials as environment variables
  5. Exposes a public HTTPS endpoint for AI assistants to connect to

The deployment uses several best practices:

  • Multi-stage Docker builds to minimize image size
  • Non-root user for improved security
  • Health checks for reliability monitoring
  • Environment-specific configurations for dev/test/prod separation

Now that our MCP server is deployed to the cloud, let's configure Claude Desktop to connect to it.

docs.title: Configuring Claude Desktop to Use the Open Horizon MCP Server
docs.text: Claude Desktop is a powerful AI assistant that can be extended with MCP servers to provide specialized capabilities. In this section, we'll configure Claude Desktop to connect to our Open Horizon MCP server, whether it's running locally or in the cloud.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before configuring Claude Desktop:

  • Install Claude Desktop on your computer (available for macOS and Windows)
  • Ensure your MCP server is running either locally or on IBM Cloud Code Engine
  • Have your Open Horizon Exchange credentials ready

docs.title: Step 1: Locate the Claude Desktop Configuration File
docs.text:
Claude Desktop stores its configuration in a JSON file. The location depends on your operating system:

  • macOS: ~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json
  • Windows: %APPDATA%\Claude\claude_desktop_config.json

docs.title: Step 2: Edit the Configuration File
docs.text:
Open the configuration file in your favorite text editor. You'll see a structure like this:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    // Existing MCP server configurations may be here
  }
}

docs.title: Step 3: Add the Open Horizon MCP Server Configuration
docs.text: Add a new entry for your Open Horizon MCP server. You have two options depending on where your server is running:

docs.title: Option A: For a Local MCP Server
docs.text:
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "open-horizon-mcp-local": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": [
        "-y", 
        "mcp-remote", 
        "http://localhost:3000/mcp",
        "--header",
        "exchange-org:your-organization",
        "--header",
        "exchange-url:http://your-exchange-url:3091/v1/orgs",
        "--header",
        "exchange-credential:your-base64-encoded-credentials"
      ]
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Option B: For a Cloud-Deployed MCP Server
docs.text:
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "open-horizon-mcp-cloud": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": [
        "-y", 
        "mcp-remote", 
        "https://your-app-name.region.codeengine.appdomain.cloud/mcp",
        "--header",
        "exchange-org:your-organization",
        "--header",
        "exchange-url:http://your-exchange-url:3091/v1/orgs",
        "--header",
        "exchange-credential:your-base64-encoded-credentials",
        "--header",
        "Authorization:Bearer your-auth-token"
      ]
    }
  }
}

Replace the placeholders with your actual values: - your-organization: Your Open Horizon organization name - your-exchange-url: The URL of your Open Horizon Exchange - your-base64-encoded-credentials: Your Base64-encoded credentials - your-app-name.region.codeengine.appdomain.cloud: The URL of your deployed Code Engine application - your-auth-token: If your MCP server requires authentication

docs.title: Step 4: Using Environment Variables for Sensitive Information
docs.text:
For better security, you can use environment variables for sensitive information:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "open-horizon-mcp": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": [
        "-y", 
        "mcp-remote", 
        "https://your-app-name.region.codeengine.appdomain.cloud/mcp",
        "--header",
        "exchange-org:playground",
        "--header",
        "exchange-url:http://your-exchange-url:3091/v1/orgs",
        "--header",
        "exchange-credential:${EXCHANGE_CREDENTIAL}",
        "--header",
        "Authorization:Bearer ${MCP_AUTH_TOKEN}"
      ],
      "env": {
        "EXCHANGE_CREDENTIAL": "your-base64-encoded-credentials",
        "MCP_AUTH_TOKEN": "your-auth-token"
      }
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Step 5: Save and Restart Claude Desktop
docs.text: After editing the configuration file, save it and restart Claude Desktop for the changes to take effect.

docs.title: Step 6: Verify the Connection
docs.text:
To verify that Claude Desktop is successfully connected to your Open Horizon MCP server:

  1. Open Claude Desktop
  2. Start a new conversation
  3. Ask Claude to list the available nodes in your Open Horizon Exchange: "List all nodes registered in the Open Horizon Exchange"

If everything is configured correctly, Claude should use the MCP server to fetch and display the list of nodes.

docs.title: Understanding How Claude Desktop Connects to MCP Servers
docs.text:
When you configure an MCP server in Claude Desktop:

  1. Claude Desktop launches a local process using the specified command and args
  2. The mcp-remote tool establishes a connection to your MCP server
  3. Claude communicates with the MCP server through this connection
  4. The MCP server authenticates with the Open Horizon Exchange using the provided credentials
  5. Claude gains access to all the tools registered in the MCP server

This architecture allows Claude to securely interact with your Open Horizon environment without needing direct access to your credentials or systems.

Now that we've configured Claude Desktop to use our MCP server, let's explore how to use it to manage your Open Horizon environment.

docs.title: Using the Open Horizon MCP Server with Claude Desktop
docs.text: Now that we have our Open Horizon MCP server running and Claude Desktop configured to use it, let's explore how to leverage this powerful combination to manage your Open Horizon environment through natural language conversations.

docs.title: Available Tools and Capabilities
docs.text: The Open Horizon MCP server provides a rich set of tools that Claude can use to help you manage your edge computing environment. These tools are grouped into three main categories:

docs.title: Node Management Tools
docs.text:
• list-nodes: List all registered nodes
  • get-node-policy: Get the policy for a specific node
  • register-node-policy: Register a node with a policy
  • unregister-node: Remove a node from the Exchange

docs.title: Service Management Tools
docs.text:
• list-services: List all available services
  • get-service-details: Get detailed information about a service
  • publish-service: Publish a new service to the Exchange
  • delete-service: Remove a service from the Exchange
  • generate-service-definition: Create a service definition template

docs.title: Policy Management Tools
docs.text:
• list-deployment-policies: List all deployment policies
  • get-policy-details: Get detailed information about a policy
  • check-policy-deployments: See which workloads use a specific policy
  • check-policy-compatibility: Check which services are compatible with a policy
  • delete-policy: Remove a policy from the Exchange

docs.title: Example Conversations with Claude
docs.text: Let's look at some example conversations that demonstrate how to use Claude with the Open Horizon MCP server for common edge computing management tasks.

docs.title: Example 1: Exploring Your Edge Environment
docs.text:
You: I'm new to Open Horizon. Can you help me understand what's in my environment?

Claude: I'd be happy to help you explore your Open Horizon environment. Let's start by checking what nodes and services you have.

First, let me list all the nodes registered in your Open Horizon Exchange:

[Claude uses the list-nodes tool and displays the results]

These are all the edge devices registered in your environment. Now, let's see what services are available:

[Claude uses the list-services tool and displays the results]

Would you like me to explain any specific node or service in more detail?

docs.title: Example 2: Deploying a Service to Edge Nodes
docs.text:
You: I want to deploy the "hello-world" service to nodes with the "location:office" property.

Claude: I'll help you deploy the "hello-world" service to nodes with the "location:office" property. This involves creating a deployment policy that targets those specific nodes.

First, let me check if the "hello-world" service exists:

[Claude uses the get-service-details tool to verify the service exists]

Now, I'll create a deployment policy that targets nodes with the "location:office" property. Here's what the policy would look like:

{
  "label": "hello-world-office-deployment",
  "description": "Deploy hello-world to office locations",
  "service": {
    "name": "hello-world",
    "org": "your-organization",
    "arch": "amd64",
    "serviceVersions": [
      {
        "version": "1.0.0",
        "priority": {
          "priority_value": 1,
          "retries": 1,
          "retry_durations": 3600
        }
      }
    ]
  },
  "constraints": [
    "location == office"
  ]
}

Would you like me to publish this deployment policy to your Exchange?

[After your confirmation, Claude would use the appropriate tools to create and publish the policy]

docs.title: Example 3: Troubleshooting Node Registration
docs.text:
You: Node "edge-device-001" isn't running the services I expected. Can you help me troubleshoot?

Claude: I'll help you troubleshoot why "edge-device-001" isn't running the expected services. Let's investigate step by step.

First, let me check if the node is registered and get its policy:

[Claude uses the get-node-policy tool to retrieve the node's policy]

Now, let's see which services should be compatible with this node based on its policy:

[Claude uses the check-policy-compatibility tool to determine compatible services]

I notice that the node's policy has constraints that might be preventing the service from deploying. The node requires "memory >= 2048" but your service is configured for "memory >= 4096".

You have two options:

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text: This document outlines the plan to extend container-converter to support docker-compose.yml files (v2.x and Docker Compose Specification) in addition to Dockerfiles. The tool will be able to parse Compose files and generate appropriate Open Horizon Service Definition Files (SDFs) for multi-container edge deployments.

docs.title: Current State Analysis
docs.text:
What container-converter supports today:

  • ✅ Single Dockerfile → Single-service SDF conversion
  • ✅ SDF type system supports multi-service structure (deployment.services is a dictionary)
  • ✅ SDF validator handles multiple services correctly
  • ✅ SDF generator creates only one service per Dockerfile

docs.title: Docker Compose Version Compatibility
docs.text:
Unified Parser Approach:

The tool uses a single parser for both Docker Compose v2.x/v3.x and the modern Compose Specification. This works because:

  1. Backward Compatibility: The Compose Specification is a superset of v2.x/v3.x formats. Core service fields (image, ports, environment, volumes, depends_on, command, entrypoint) are identical across all versions.

  2. Feature Extraction: We only extract fields that:

  3. Exist in all Compose versions
  4. Map directly to Open Horizon SDF ServiceConfig

  5. Are relevant for edge deployments

  6. Version Field Handling: The deprecated version field (v2.x/v3.x) triggers an informational warning but doesn't block parsing. The parser successfully processes files with or without this field.

  7. Version-Specific Features We Ignore:

  8. v2.x resource limits (cpu_shares, mem_limit) - not extracted
  9. v3.x deploy configs (deploy.replicas, deploy.resources) - not relevant for single-node edge
  10. Network drivers - Open Horizon manages networking

Testing: The test suite includes v2-legacy.docker-compose.yml fixture that validates v2.4 files parse correctly alongside modern Compose Specification files.

Open Horizon Multi-Container Architecture:

Based on research and the EdgeX Kamakura example, Open Horizon supports two approaches:

  1. Single SDF with Multiple Containers - The deployment.services field can contain multiple service definitions in one SDF
  2. Multiple SDFs + Pattern - Separate SDFs published individually, then grouped via a Pattern for orchestration (recommended for complex deployments)

Real-world example from EdgeX Kamakura:

Each service (consul, redis, mqtt-broker, etc.) has its own service.definition.json:

{
  "deployment": {
    "services": {
      "consul": {
        "image": "hashicorp/consul:1.15",
        "command": ["agent", "-ui", "-bootstrap"],
        "ports": [{ "HostPort": "8500:8500/tcp" }],
        "binds": ["/data/consul:/consul/data:rw"]
      }
    }
  },
  "requiredServices": [{ "url": "deploy-data", "version": "1.0.0" }]
}

Then, services are orchestrated using patterns that reference multiple services:

{
  "services": [
    { "serviceUrl": "asc-mqtt", "serviceVersions": [{ "version": "1.0.0" }] },
    { "serviceUrl": "edgex-ui", "serviceVersions": [{ "version": "1.0.0" }] }
  ]
}

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
1. Parse docker-compose.yml files (v2.x and Compose Spec)
  2. Generate valid Open Horizon SDFs from Compose files
  3. Support both single-SDF (simple cases) and multi-SDF (complex cases) generation strategies
  4. Map Compose concepts (networks, volumes, depends_on) to Open Horizon concepts
  5. Provide clear CLI options for different generation strategies
  6. Maintain backward compatibility with Dockerfile-only conversion

docs.title: Non-Goals
docs.text:
• Full Docker Compose feature parity (only features mappable to Open Horizon)
  • Runtime Compose execution (only SDF generation)
  • Automated Docker registry management
  • Pattern generation (will be future enhancement)
